title: AQA English Language Paper 1 Question 2: How to Analyse Language
description: How to answer AQA GCSE English Language Paper 1 Question 2: an 8-mark language analysis method, mini-example, common mistakes and practice checklist.

children: Question 2 is the first substantial analysis task on AQA GCSE English Language Paper 1. It is worth 8 marks and assesses AO2: how well you can explain, comment on and analyse the writer’s use of language. The strongest answers do not collect techniques. They make a precise point, choose useful evidence and explain how particular language choices create meaning or an effect.
What the question is really testing
Can you select a short, relevant quotation from the specified lines?
Can you analyse a word, phrase or language choice rather than simply paraphrasing it?
Can you explain how that choice contributes to the impression, mood, character or idea named in the question?
Can you use terminology accurately when it genuinely helps the analysis?
A useful rule: technique is the label; analysis is the thinking. Naming a metaphor is not valuable unless you explain what the metaphor makes the reader understand.
A reliable five-step method
Read the focus of the question first. Decide exactly what impression or effect you are being asked to explore.
Choose a compact quotation that contains a word or phrase you can genuinely unpack. Long quotations usually create more work, not more marks.
Make a clear inference about the writer’s choice. Ask: what does this word suggest here?
Develop the analysis. Consider connotations, associations, intensity, contrast, imagery, tone or a second plausible interpretation.
Return to the question. Explain how the language contributes to the named focus rather than ending with a vague statement about the reader.
Mini-example: move from spotting to analysis

Imagine the invented sentence: “The corridor swallowed the last strip of daylight.” A weak comment would say that “swallowed” is personification. A stronger response explains that the verb makes the corridor seem predatory and active, as though darkness is consuming the remaining safety. The image therefore makes the setting feel increasingly threatening rather than merely dark.
The improvement comes from following the implication of the word. The term “personification” is accurate, but the mark-worthy part is the explanation of what the choice suggests.
Common reasons answers stay in the middle
Feature spotting: “The writer uses a metaphor.” Nothing is said about the meaning created.
Paraphrase: the quotation is repeated in different words without analysing the writer’s choice.
Generic effects: “This makes the reader want to read on” is attached to almost every quotation.
Over-analysis without relevance: a word is explored at length but the response loses the question’s actual focus.
One undeveloped paragraph: one good idea is better than several weak ones, but an 8-mark response still needs enough developed evidence to show a range of understanding.
A 10-minute practice drill
Choose four lines from an unseen fiction extract.
Underline one phrase that creates a clear impression.
Write one sentence stating the impression.
Write two sentences analysing one important word or image.
Add a final sentence linking the choice back to the question focus.
Repeat with a second quotation, then compare which paragraph contains the more precise analysis.
Final check before moving on
I answered the exact focus of the question.
My quotations are short and relevant.
I analysed choices rather than translating them.
Any terminology I used is accurate and useful.
My effects are specific to this text, not generic reader-effect phrases.
